title: STAR EXCLUSIVE: OCT. 30, 2000 - THE KILLING OF ROBERT CARPENTER - Cops, widow at odds over shooting death; Was Amherstburg man armed? Inquest to decide
article: The story Lisa Stewart will weave at the inquest into her husband's shooting death will differ dramatically from the version accepted by the investigators who cleared police of any wrongdoing.

The province's special investigations unit, the civilian agency that probes police shootings, concluded, after eight investigators interviewed 10 civilians and four witness police officers during a three-week probe, that the use of "lethal force" was "legally justified."

In Stewart's version, one the eyewitness is aching to recount for a coroner's jury, the police officer who shot and killed her husband was not in uniform and no police officer was ever in physical danger.
In her version, her common-law husband did not lunge at a police officer with a knife and he certainly didn't slash at a downed officer.
In her version, there was no knife.
It will be up to a coroner's jury to decide which version represents the truth.
Stewart's husband, Robert Scott Carpenter, 36, was shot and killed by an unidentified Amherstburg police officer shortly after 7 a.m. Oct. 30.

Carpenter, the father of Stewart's two children, was shot near the groin in his right femoral artery and collapsed on the front lawn of the couple's home. He was rushed to Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital and pronounced dead three hours later.
Amherstburg police officers arrived at the couple's three- bedroom home at 258 McCurdy Dr., after receiving what is called a "disrupted" 911 call.
Stewart says she made the call because Carpenter was acting erratically but then had second thoughts and hung up the phone.

According to the sequence of events outlined in the SIU ruling -- the facts of which are disputed by Stewart and Patrick Ducharme, the lawyer for Carpenter's family -- the officers arrived at the house to find a highly charged domestic dispute.

The SIU concluded a uniformed officer arrived to find Stewart distraught and requesting assistance. Carpenter was inside the house with his two children and refused to open the door. Two officers, one of them not in uniform, arrived in a backup role and joined their comrade on the front porch.

The SIU ruling said the door suddenly opened and that one of the officers fell to the floor and was set upon by a knife-wielding Carpenter. When Carpenter refused to drop the weapon and persisted in the assault, another officer shot and killed him.
The SIU wouldn't confirm whether the shooter was in or out of uniform. Stewart maintains he wasn't wearing a uniform.

With the inquest just weeks away, Stewart would only outline the broadstrokes of what happened when the police arrived at the home she shared with Carpenter for more than three years. And those broadstrokes are substantially different from the conclusions reached by the SIU.

Stewart says the first officer arrived at the door and Carpenter opened the door and refused to let him in. When she pleaded for him to get her outside, the officer grabbed her arm, Carpenter grabbed another and a tug-of-war ensued.
Stewart says the officer managed to pull her outside although she stumbled in the process and broke her rib. She says a non-uniformed police officer then arrived at the scene.
Stewart won't detail the events that unfolded immediately before the shooting or what exactly triggered the fatal bullet to be fired.
She is adamant, however, that Carpenter was not armed with a knife; a startling departure from the official version of events.
Two police officers suffered non-life-threatening injuries in the incident which included a cut to the face of one of them.
Stewart says the cuts were caused by a mirror which broke in the front foyer of their home.
Citing the coming inquest, Amherstburg police Chief Brian Bird politely declined to respond to questions about Stewart's version of events.
He confirmed the officers involved in the shooting were back on the job after an unspecified time off on stress leave.
"It goes without saying that it's a difficult time for everyone and it always has been," said Bird about the mood of his 29-member police force.
He said he welcomed the pending inquest as a means of preventing similar incidents.
"I think this inquest is a necessary probe.
"Hopefully we can learn many things from it. That's what an inquest is all about," he said.

The coroner's inquest into the shooting death of Robert Carpenter will take place July 3. It is expected to last two weeks and hear from approximately 26 witnesses. Dr. Thomas Wilson, regional supervising coroner, will preside over the inquest, which will review the events surrounding the death and may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar tragedies. It will begin 10 a.m. at Duffy's Marina, 306 Dalhousie St., in Amherstburg.
